title: Connected Objects and Tension
short: Treat linked objects as one system to find a, then one object alone to find the tension.
trouble: Students think the rope's tension equals the applied force or the hanging weight.

blocks.html: Trains of carts, a block pulled by a hanging weight, two boxes pushed together: the objects move together, so they share one acceleration. The trick is choosing the right system for each question, then using Newton's Second Law Along an Axis.

To find the shared acceleration, treat all the linked objects as one system: the forces between them are internal and cancel. To find a rope tension or a contact force, take one object alone: then that force is external and appears in its equation.

Each choice of system leaves out different forces. The whole train hides the ropes between the cars, so its equation has only the outside pull and the total mass. A single car shows its rope as an ordinary force. Both equations are true at once, and using them in that order gives each unknown with the least algebra.

blocks.title: Two carts and a rope
blocks.q: On a frictionless track you pull a $3\ \text{kg}$ cart with $20\ \text{N}$; a rope links it to a $2\ \text{kg}$ cart behind. Find $a$ and the tension.
steps: Rear cart alone: the rope is its only horizontal force, so $T = (2)(4) = 8\ \text{N}$.

blocks.title: A hanging weight
blocks.q: A $4\ \text{kg}$ block on a frictionless table is tied over a light pulley to a hanging $1\ \text{kg}$ block. Find $a$ and $T$.
steps: System along the string: the only unbalanced force is the hanging weight, $9.8\ \text{N}$, moving $5\ \text{kg}$ in all.
Table block alone: $T = (4)(1.96) = 7.84\ \text{N}$, less than the hanging block's $9.8\ \text{N}$ weight.

blocks.html: Thinking a rope's tension equals the applied force, or equals the hanging weight. The rope only has to accelerate what is behind it, so its tension is a fraction of the pull; and if a hanging block is accelerating downward, the rope must pull up on it with less than its weight. Check: compare your tension with the forces on each side of the rope; it should fall between them.
